questions.stem: Which of the following best defines globalisation?
options: The increasing integration and interdependence of national economies through trade, investment, migration and information flows
The growth of international trade in goods
The spread of one country's culture across the world
The formation of trading blocs between neighbouring countries
questions.why: A trade-only definition loses marks, because globalisation includes investment, migration and information.
whyNot: Trade is only one dimension.
Cultural spread is a consequence, not the definition.
Blocs are one regional form of integration.

questions.stem: How is the openness of an economy measured?
options: ((Exports + Imports) / GDP) x 100
((Exports - Imports) / GDP) x 100
(Exports / Imports) x 100
(GDP / (Exports + Imports)) x 100
questions.why: Openness measures the size of trade flows relative to the economy, so exports and imports are added.
whyNot: That is the trade balance as a share of GDP.
That is a ratio of exports to imports.
That inverts the calculation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines foreign direct investment?
options: Investment by a firm in productive assets in another country, usually with a controlling interest
The purchase of foreign shares and bonds for a financial return
A loan from one government to another
The value of a country's exports of capital goods
questions.why: FDI is long-term, brings technology and management, and is hard to withdraw quickly.
whyNot: That is portfolio investment.
That is intergovernmental lending or aid.
That is a trade flow.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a remittance?
options: Money sent home by a worker living abroad
A payment made by a government to a foreign supplier
Interest paid on foreign debt
Profit repatriated by a multinational
questions.why: Remittances are recorded as secondary income on the current account and exceed aid for several economies.
whyNot: That is an import payment.
That is debt service, recorded as primary income.
That is also primary income, not a remittance.

questions.stem: GDP is $420bn, exports are $118bn and imports are $146bn. What is the openness of the economy?
whyNot: That uses exports minus imports, which measures the trade balance.
That uses exports and imports separately in error.
That inverts part of the calculation.

questions.stem: Using the same figures, what is the trade balance?
options: A deficit of $28bn
A surplus of $28bn
A deficit of $264bn
A surplus of $264bn
questions.why: 118 - 146 = -$28bn, a deficit. Note that this is a completely different measure from openness.
whyNot: Imports exceed exports, so it is a deficit.
That adds the two figures, which gives total trade.
That adds the two figures and mislabels the result.

questions.stem: Why is openness typically higher for a small economy than a large one?
options: A small economy cannot produce everything, while a large one can trade internally
Small economies always have lower tariffs
Large economies do not record their trade accurately
Small economies always run trade surpluses
questions.why: Comparison of openness between countries must allow for size, or the figure is misread.
whyNot: Tariff levels vary independently of size.
Large economies record trade carefully.
Many small economies run deficits.

questions.stem: Which of the following distinguishes FDI from portfolio investment?
options: FDI involves productive assets and a controlling interest and is hard to withdraw quickly
FDI is always larger in value
Portfolio investment is illegal in developing countries
FDI is recorded in the current account
questions.why: Portfolio investment is mobile and can leave overnight, which is the capital flight problem.
whyNot: Size does not define the category.
Portfolio investment is lawful and widespread.
Both are financial account flows.

questions.stem: What does intra-firm trade mean, and why does it matter?
options: Components move between subsidiaries of the same company, which creates the scope for transfer pricing
Firms trade only with their competitors, which raises prices
Governments trade on behalf of firms, which distorts statistics
Firms trade only within their own country, which reduces openness
questions.why: It also makes trade statistics harder to interpret, because a good crossing three borders during assembly is counted three times.
whyNot: Intra-firm means within one group.
Most trade is conducted by private firms.
Intra-firm trade crosses borders, which is why it is trade.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an effect of migration on the sending country?
options: Remittances flow in, and skilled workers are lost, which is the brain drain
The dependency ratio always falls permanently
Unemployment always rises
Total world output falls
questions.why: The country pays to train workers whose productivity then benefits another economy, offset by remittance inflows.
whyNot: Emigration of working-age people can raise the dependency ratio.
Emigration usually relieves unemployment.
Migration raises world output, because labour moves to where it is more productive.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most balanced statement about migration?
options: It raises world output, and its costs and benefits are distributed very unevenly
It benefits every country involved equally
It harms both the sending and receiving countries
It has no measurable economic effects
questions.why: The distributional point is what earns the evaluation marks in a migration question.
whyNot: The effects are highly uneven between and within countries.
Total output rises, so it cannot harm everyone.
The effects on output, wages and remittances are substantial.

questions.stem: For a small open economy with a high import content, what is the most useful framing?
options: Globalisation is the environment rather than a policy choice
Globalisation can be avoided by raising tariffs
Globalisation affects only the export sector
Openness can be reduced without reducing living standards
questions.why: Where almost all goods are imported, global prices transmit directly into the domestic economy with nothing to absorb the shock.
whyNot: Tariffs raise the cost of essential imports rather than removing the exposure.
Import dependence affects the whole economy.
Reducing openness in such an economy would sharply reduce living standards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of globalisation named in the specification?
options: An increase in migration
A fall in world interest rates
The convergence of tax rates between countries
A rise in government spending as a share of GDP
questions.why: The three named characteristics are trade rising as a share of GDP, the growing importance of TNCs and FDI, and rising migration.
whyNot: Interest rates are not a named characteristic.
Tax competition is a consequence discussed elsewhere.
Public spending growth has other causes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a transnational company?
options: A company that owns or controls production or service operations in more than one country
A company that exports to more than one country
A company owned by shareholders of several nationalities
A company listed on more than one stock exchange
questions.why: Ownership or control of operations abroad is the defining feature, not simply selling abroad.
whyNot: That is an exporter.
Shareholder nationality is not the test.
Multiple listing is a financing arrangement.

questions.stem: A country's openness figure is 62.9% while its trade balance is in deficit. What does this show?
options: The economy is heavily integrated into world trade and imports exceed exports
The economy is closed and imports exceed exports
The economy is heavily integrated and exports exceed imports
The two figures are inconsistent with each other
questions.why: Openness measures the size of trade flows; the balance measures the difference between them. Confusing the two is the commonest error.
whyNot: A figure of 62.9% indicates a very open economy.
A deficit means imports exceed exports.
They measure different things and are entirely consistent.

questions.stem: Why does FDI create a permanent negative entry on the current account of the host country?
options: Repatriated profits are recorded as a debit on primary income each year
The initial investment is a current account debit
Imported inputs are recorded as secondary income
FDI is not recorded in the balance of payments
questions.why: The initial investment is a financial account inflow; the profits it later generates flow out through primary income annually.
whyNot: The investment itself is a financial account flow.
Imported inputs are current account debits under trade, not secondary income.
All of it is recorded.
